rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract : AI has the potential to bring much-needed acceleration to the development of chemicals and materials for energy and sustainability, just like it has delivered intelligence gains in other fields. The path to success goes through scaling, perhaps exclusively through scaling. Rich Sutton's 'bitter lesson' states that "general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective" in AI. The corollaries are bittersweet in chemistry and materials. The lesson permeates through the use of AI in chemistry and materials. The tremendous success of universal ML interatomic potentials (MLIPs) as surrogate for quantum-mechanical energies and forces is unarguable. Trained on 100-million-count datasets, they reflect scaling laws similar to the ones in language or vision models, generalizing to new scientific questions and enabling simulations that were intractable a few years ago. Generative models, trained mostly on the same synthetic data, are currently being used to propose novel materials at machine speed. The discussion around the power of inductive bias (energy conservation, equivariance) and whether it is better reflected in model architecture or in training strategy is very much ongoing. The physical sciences may well be the last holdout for domain knowledge and inductive bias, or maybe they will ultimately follow the same trends as other domains. But MLIPs are surrogates for physics-based simulators, and arguably, materials only truly matter if they are made in the lab and then scaled up industrially and commercially. This is the truly bitter scaling lesson in materials. The promise of AI for chemistry and materials needs to be realized through very traditional, expensive and slow channels. In this talk, I will describe our group's work both in the highly scalable fusion of simulations and machine learning, and in the "high-contact" and lower throughput effort of translating AI designs into tangible, scalable products, in areas like heterogeneous catalysis, battery materials or sustainable polymers Bio: Rafael Gomez-Bombarelli is the Paul M Cook Associate Professor in MIT's Department of Materials Science and Engineering; and co-founder and Chief Scientific Officer at Lila Sciences. He earned his undergraduate and graduate degrees in chemistry from the University of Salamanca, Spain, and conducted postdoctoral research at Heriot-Watt University and Harvard University, under Alan Aspuru-Guzik. Rafa's research integrates machine learning with atomistic simulations to expedite the discovery and design of novel materials for applications in energy, sustainability, and healthcare.

title: Test-Time Scaling Makes Overtraining Compute-Optimal
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video Abstract Modern LLMs scale at test-time, e.g. via repeated sampling, where inference cost grows with model size and the number of samples. This creates a trade-off that pretraining scaling laws, such as Chinchilla, do not address. In this talk, we present Train-to-Test (T^2) scaling laws that jointly optimize model size, training tokens, and number of inference samples under fixed end-to-end budgets. T^2 modernizes pretraining scaling laws with pass@k modeling used for test-time scaling, then jointly optimizes pretraining and test-time decisions. Forecasts from T^2 are robust over distinct modeling approaches: measuring joint scaling effect on the task loss and modeling impact on task accuracy. Across eight downstream tasks, we find that when accounting for inference cost, optimal pretraining decisions shift radically into the overtraining regime, well-outside of the range of standard pretraining scaling suites. We validate our results by pretraining heavily overtrained models in the optimal region that T^2 scaling forecasts, confirming their substantially stronger performance compared to pretraining scaling alone. Finally, as frontier LLMs are post-trained, we show that our findings survive the post-training stage, making T^2 scaling meaningful in modern deployments. Link to Bio: https://nick11roberts.science/ Sponsor Event organized by PLI Special Event Seminar Lunch Series

title: Do Thinking Tokens Help with Safety?
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video Abstract : Today's reasoning models use thinking tokens to attain stronger performance on benchmarks than their instruction-tuned counterparts. It is also generally believed that this more "deliberative" mode should improve alignment and safety, by providing the model a safe space to consider whether its planned answer to a request violates its safety principles. We present evidence that this intuition is not always correct. Across frontier open-weight reasoning models spanning GPT-OSS, Qwen, Olmo, and Phi families, we find that the eventual refusal/compliance outcome is already strongly predictable via a trained head on the first token's hidden representation (0.84-0.95 AUROC and ∼88% balanced accuracy for predicting refusal/compliance) before any visible thinking. The thinking process turns out to be more akin to prefix completion than to deliberative revision, with the final outcome rarely changing after the first ∼20% of thinking, despite giving the appearance of deliberation at the text level (∼74% of text-level deliberations occur when the response distribution is already locked to one refusal/compliance side). We also find that existing inference-time and training-based safety interventions, despite being motivated by the goal of inducing deliberation, largely shift model behavior toward over-refusal while suppressing already-scarce deliberation signals. Our results suggest that safety behavior in current reasoning models is much less deliberative than commonly assumed, and highlight the need for methods that induce real safety deliberation. Bio : Narutatsu Ri is a second-year Ph.D. student advised by Professor Sanjeev Arora. His research focuses on the safety and alignment of large foundation models, with particular interests in measuring and mitigating misalignment, scalable oversight, and the safety implications of self-improving AI systems. title: Whose AI for Amazon Forests? Technological Sovereignty for Indigenizing Science
content: The study for this talk traces the techno-scientific and political-economic trajectory of the development and use of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) model that simulates, monitors and predicts Amazonian deforestation. Developed mainly by Brazilian scientists, this model has been used for scientific research, policymaking, and forest conservation. However, in the process of international validation of this REDD+ carbon accounting
rawEventDetails: Speaker Shaozeng Zhang Affiliation Associate Professor of Anthropology, Oregon State University; PLAS Visiting Fellow, Princeton University Details Event Description The study for this talk traces the techno-scientific and political-economic trajectory of the development and use of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) model that simulates, monitors and predicts Amazonian deforestation. Developed mainly by Brazilian scientists, this model has been used for scientific research, policymaking, and forest conservation. It also provided the technical foundation for South America’s first REDD+ forest carbon project and the world’s first REDD+ carbon accounting methodology. However, in the process of international validation of this REDD+ carbon accounting methodology, the validation agencies, all from Europe and North America, imposed technical requirements, such as smaller Minimum Mapping Units and higher satellite-imaging resolution, that were disconnected from the geographical scales and technological capacities of tropical rainforest countries. These requirements practically make Brazilian scientists lose control over rainforest data, technical standards, and knowledge validity. They also forced the world’s tropical rainforest countries to reply on European and North American data infrastructures and AI models, continuously paying high transaction costs in global carbon markets and environmental governance. Based on long-term ethnographic work among Brazilian scientists and technocrats since 2009, Shaozeng Zhang uses their growing concern with “technological sovereignty” as an emic anthropological concept. Zhang analyzes how AI development and use are constrained by knowledge hegemony and North-South inequality in the postcolonial world. Finally, moving beyond political-economic or ethical debates, Zhang suggests an epistemologically reflexive approach of decolonizing or indigenizing science for better human knowledge production today. ABOUT OUR GUEST SPEAKER Shaozeng Zhang (Ph.D., University of California, Irvine), is Associate Professor of Anthropology, and affiliated professor of humanitarian engineering, at Oregon State University. His research focuses on Amazon forest conservation, climate change adaptation, science and technology studies, big data and artificial intelligence, and mixed-methods innovations. He has published in anthropology journals such as Economic Anthropology , Annals of Anthropological Practice, Teaching Anthropology, and Antropologia Portuguesa, as well as multidisciplinary journals such as Engineering Studies, Methodological Innovations, Annals of the American Association of Geographers, and Tapuya: Latin American Science, Technology and Society. He has been awarded research funding from various agencies, including the U.S. National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Wenner-Gren Foundation. He also served as a Junior Visiting Scholar in the Department of Anthropology at the University of Brasilia ( Universidade de Brasília ) in Brazil. At Princeton, Zhang will continue developing a carbon-aware and co-evolving human-AI framework for Amazon deforestation monitoring in partnership with computer scientists, Princeton scholars, and Brazilian researchers. DISCUSSANT Lucas Prates, Lecturer, Department of Anthropology, Princeton University This event is co-sponsored by the Department of Anthropology. This event is open to students, faculty, visiting scholars and staff. Sponsorship of an event does not constitute institutional endorsement of external speakers or views presented.

title: Open Questions in AI Benchmarking
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Video Abstract: In this talk I will lay out what I take to be some of the big open questions about AI capabilities. These questions govern the impact that AI will have on the world. I'll also discuss some of the work being done (at my company and by others) to build benchmarks that help answer these questions. Short bio : Greg Burnham is the head of benchmarks at Epoch AI. Prior to this, he worked at Elemental Cognition and Bridgewater Associates. He has a BA in mathematics from Princeton University. title: DARK MANSIONS: AI, Innovation, and Fermat’s Last Theorem
rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Yiu, Kosoy, and Gopnik (2024) argue that “Cultural evolution depends on a fine balance between imitation and innovation.” Writing in a world prior to reasoning models, they argued that large language models fall squarely on the imitation side. This paper—focused principally on formal and scientific innovation—proposes a finer-grained, three-tier taxonomy: Tier 1 is transmission, Tier 2 is something new (invention) within a fixed problem formulation, and Tier 3 is framework-generating innovation. Tier 3 requires both historical novelty—a new construction or framework—and functional novelty—a downstream dividend, where the apparatus introduced to solve a problem helps to reorganize later work. We explore Andrew Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem as a case of Tier 3 innovation. Core elements of the proof architecture—especially the R = T modularity-lifting strategy and Taylor–Wiles patching—were not present in the prior mathematical literature. Moreover, the proof apparatus has had substantial downstream impact on number theory and the Langlands program. We consider whether a current frontier AI system trained on pre‑1987 mathematical sources could have produced a Wiles-type proof strategy, and offer reasons for doubt. Broadening the argument beyond the Wiles proof, we analyze three current AI paradigms for AI in mathematics and argue that they do not yet offer clear mechanisms for Tier 3 innovation. We then assess the empirical record of AI-assisted mathematical discovery, including the refutation of the unit-distance conjecture and the proof of the existence of non-sofic groups. We find a growing number of striking Tier 2 achievements, but no evidence yet of Tier 3 innovation. Tier 3 innovation, we propose, depends on three capacities—imagination, judgment, and tenacity, understood functionally as capacities for novel decomposition, structural evaluation, and sustained exploration. Current architectures have not shown these capacities at the scale required for Tier 3 innovation. The paper concludes with reflections on the architectural changes that may be needed for the innovation that comes from what Andrew Wiles vividly describes as stumbling around in “dark mansions.” Bio: Joshua Cohen is a political philosopher. He has written on issues of democratic theory, freedom of expression, religious freedom, political equality, democracy and digital technology, good jobs, and global justice. His books include On Democracy (with Joel Rogers); Democracy and Associations ( with Joel Rogers); Philosophy, Politics, Democracy ; Rousseau: A Free Community of Equals ; and The Arc of the Moral Universe and Other Essays . He is co-editor of the Norton Introduction to Philosophy , now in its third edition. Cohen taught at MIT (1977-2005), Stanford (2005-2014), is currently on the faculty at Apple University, and is Distinguished Senior Fellow in Law, Philosophy, and Political Science at University of California, Berkeley. Cohen held the Romanell-Phi Beta Kappa Professorship in 2002-3; gave the Tanner Lectures at UC Berkeley in 2007; the Comte Lectures at LSE in 2012; and the Annual Lecture on Ethics and AI at Oxford in 2024. He is co-editor-in-chief of Boston Review . This talk will be recorded and livestreamed. The recording will be posted to the CITP website, the CITP YouTube channel and the University Media Central channel. title: DaIS Launch & Faculty Research Collaboration Symposium

location.name: Frist Health Center - A78B McLain Pavilion

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Join us for the official launch of Princeton’s Data and Intelligent Systems (DaIS), an initiative dedicated to supporting and expanding AI, Data Science, and Statistics research and education across the university. This event will introduce the DaIS vision and host a collaborative faculty symposium designed to foster interdisciplinary research partnerships. Event Details Date: September 30, 2026 Location: Frist Health Center - A78B McLain Pavilion The Launch: Introducing DaIS The event begins with a university-wide introduction to DaIS. This session will feature: Provost Jen Rexford to provide opening remarks. Tom Griffiths, Director of DaIS, will share insights on Princeton AI. Arthur Spirling, Director of DaIS, will share insights on Princeton Statistics and Data Science, and the education efforts of DaIS Faculty Research Collaboration Symposium Following the introductory remarks, the Faculty Research Collaboration Symposium will commence. This portion of the event is specifically for faculty members to present their research ideas and seek guidance and feedback from across disciplines on how AI and data science can support their work. The aim is to help create new productive collaborations among colleagues across the university. In addition, faculty previously in receipt of DaIS seed grants will present work that flowed from those efforts. Reception The conclusion of the event invites all to a light reception to mingle and connect with peers.
